dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper addresses the challenge of generating privacy-preserving synthetic financial data in a setting where data integrity and privacy regulations hinder access to real data, focusing on oversampling an extremely imbalanced minority class of approved withdrawal requests in a Banco BV FGTS approval dataset. Synthetic data is framed as a way to protect sensitive training data while correcting class imbalance for downstream modelling. The authors also position their work within the broader question of whether near-term quantum generative models can handle complex real-world financial datasets.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The study proposes and implements a hybrid quantum-classical GAN (HQGAN) where a resource-efficient quantum circuit acts as the generator and a classical neural network with one hidden layer serves as the discriminator. The quantum generator follows a Huang et al.-inspired design using angle-embedded QNNs with a feature map and parameterized ansatz, linear controlled-Z entanglement, and a split between data qubits for feature generation and ancilla qubits to introduce nonlinearity via partial measurement and dependence of the post-measurement state on the latent vector. Due to the 2^NG capacity constraint, the authors use NG=4 data qubits and NA=1 ancilla qubit, pad the feature space to 16 dimensions, and train the HQGAN with SGD and BCE loss in a simulator environment.

dimension_3_key_results.text: The HQGAN failed to reach sufficient accuracy to capture the complex patterns in the financial data, exhibiting erratic MSE behavior without clear convergence toward the real data distribution. In contrast, the classical GAN displayed typical loss dynamics and a consistent reduction in MSE that eventually stabilized, highlighting that in this case the hybrid quantum approach underperformed on the financial dataset. The authors reiterate in the conclusion that the HQGAN did not achieve adequate accuracy for the target financial application.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The paper explicitly compares the HQGAN against a fully classical GAN based on DCGAN, noting that the classical model has orders of magnitude more parameters and includes batch normalization, while the HQGAN has a much smaller parameter count and lacks such normalization. Empirically, the classical GAN shows typical adversarial training behavior with generator and discriminator losses remaining close and an MSE that improves and stabilizes, whereas the HQGAN's MSE is higher and erratic and does not show convergence. The authors thus report that, under their settings, the classical GAN is more effective for financial synthetic data generation than their HQGAN.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors highlight that their HQGAN could not achieve the accuracy needed to learn intricate financial patterns and generalize to the complex financial dataset, underscoring current limitations of quantum-inspired methods for such data. They point out a structural constraint in the quantum generator, whose data capacity is limited by the number of data qubits (2^NG), which forced padding of features and may restrict scalability to richer datasets. They also note that the patch strategy from the reference design was omitted due to the relatively small number of features, and they acknowledge that the absence of batch normalization in the hybrid model may cause unstable training, slower convergence, and inferior sample quality. More broadly, they frame the work within the open question of whether existing quantum devices can support real-world generative learning, implicitly noting that their results suggest current approaches are not yet adequate for this financial task.

dimension_6_future_work.text: For future work, the authors propose exploring new normalization mechanisms tailored to quantum models to address training instabilities, and investigating alternative hybrid GAN architectures in which the quantum component is placed in the discriminator or replaced by a fully quantum GAN. These directions aim to better exploit potential advantages of quantum generative models while mitigating the limitations observed in the present HQGAN design.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The contribution centers on formulating and experimentally evaluating a hybrid quantum-classical GAN with a resource-efficient quantum generator for privacy-preserving synthetic oversampling in a real-world, highly imbalanced financial approval dataset, and on empirically assessing its capability relative to a strong classical GAN baseline. By implementing a Huang et al.-inspired QNN generator with ancilla-enabled nonlinearity and adapting it to tabular financial data with specific preprocessing and padding, the paper sheds light on the near-term feasibility and limitations of quantum generative models in financial services.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the study uses a large, proprietary Banco BV FGTS approval dataset with severe class imbalance (~0.4% positives) and performs structured preprocessing including feature selection, removal of the target and time variables, ordinal encoding of a categorical feature, and min–max normalization, plus feature padding to satisfy quantum generator constraints. Both HQGAN and classical GAN are trained under a shared protocol with BCE loss, identical batch size and epochs, and performance is quantitatively evaluated using mean squared error between real and synthetic distributions. The authors also design a follow-up truncated training experiment to probe divergence behavior, indicating some effort to diagnose training instability and overfitting.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The paper notes that, because the dataset has relatively few features, the patch-based generator strategy from the reference quantum architecture was deemed unnecessary, which affects how directly their implementation aligns with prior quantum patch-GAN designs but is not central to the main findings.
